```{r data-king-lists, message=FALSE}
king_lists <- read_xlsx(here("data", "king-lists.xlsx"), col_types = "text", n_max = 75) |>
  select(-c(archetype)) |>
  pivot_longer(!c(Ruler, variants), names_to = "specimen") |>
  mutate(
    value = replace_na(value, "―"), # character absent
    value = na_if(value, "#"),# 
    value = na_if(value, "?") # lemmas
  ) |>
  filter(specimen != "MintMus1983.172.40") |> # Too many NAs
  pivot_wider(id_cols = specimen, names_from = c(Ruler, variants)) |>
  mutate(across(-specimen, as.factor))
```

This document describes the cladistic analysis of Maya king lists from our forthcoming paper:

> Helmke, Christophe, Vepretskii, Sergei, and Roe, Joe. in prep. Towards a Textual Criticism of Classic Maya Historical Sources.

The analysis used `r nrow(king_lists)` king lists, described in terms of `r ncol(king_lists) - 1` categorical traits.
One known specimen (MintMus1983.172.40) was excluded as it is only partially recorded.
The analysis was performed in `r R.version$version.string` [@R2025] and visualised with ggtree [@YuEtAl2017; @Yu2020; @Yu2022].

There are several methods we can use to generate a dendrogram of this data:
the simplest, hierarchical clustering, only considers the relative 'dissimilarity' between specimens;
the unrooted phylogenetic tree introduces the assumption that these dissimilarities are the result of a process of copying-with-error;
the rooted phylogenetic tree further assumes that specimen K1372 is the most conservative copy.

## Hierarchical clustering

Hierarchical clustering, based only on the dissimilarity between specimens.

```{r hclust}
king_lists <- column_to_rownames(king_lists, "specimen")
king_lists_dist <- hammingdists(king_lists)
king_lists_hclust <- hclust(king_lists_dist)
king_lists_hclust$labels <- rownames(king_lists)
```

```{r fig-hclust}
#| fig-cap: Dendrogram from hierarchical clustering
ggtree(king_lists_hclust, layout = "roundrect", branch.length = "none") +
  geom_tiplab() +
  hexpand(0.01)
```

## Unrooted phylogenetic tree

If we incorporate the assumption that dissimilarities between specimens arose through a process of copying with error (either from each other or from the original), we can generate a more informative tree using phylogenetic methods.
We use the 'branch and bound' algorithm [@HendyPenny1982] to find the most parsimonious trees, i.e. those that require the least number of copying errors.
Branch length, indicating the intervening dissimilarity between nodes, was calculated using Grafen's [-@Grafen1989] method.
Phylogenetic analyses were conducted using the R packages ape [@ParadisSchliep2019] and phangorn [@Schliep2011].

```{r phylo}
king_lists_phydata <- phyDat(
  as.matrix(mutate(king_lists, across(everything(), as.numeric))),
  type = "USER",
  levels = c(0:max(sapply(king_lists, as.numeric), na.rm = TRUE), NA)
)
king_lists_phylo <- bab(king_lists_phydata)
```

This results in `r length(king_lists_phylo)` most parsimonious trees.
From these we derive the consensus tree, which only includes clades that are found in all most parsiminous trees.

```{r fig-phylo}
#| fig-cap: Unrooted consensus phylogenetic tree
king_lists_phylo |>
  consensus() |>
  compute.brlen(method = "Grafen", power = 1) |>
  ggtree(layout = "roundrect") +
  geom_tiplab() +
  hexpand(0.01)
```

The consistency index and retention index are two methods of quantifying how well the observed data fits a phylogenetic model.
Both are on a scale of 0 to 1, with 1 being the most 'tree-like'.
For the consensus tree, the consistency index is `r round(CI(consensus(king_lists_phylo), king_lists_phydata), 2)` and the retention index is `r round(RI(consensus(king_lists_phylo), king_lists_phydata), 2)`.
This is within the typical range for cultural phylogenies [@CollardEtAl2006].

## Rooted phylogenetic tree

Further assuming that K1372 is the most conservative copy allows us to 'root' the trees above, i.e. ensure that this specimen is the first branch.

```{r phylo-rooted}
king_lists_phylo_rooted <- root(
  king_lists_phylo, 
  outgroup = "1372",
  resolve.root = TRUE,
  edgelabel = TRUE
)

king_lists_phylo_con <- consensus(king_lists_phylo_rooted, rooted = TRUE)
king_lists_phylo_con <- makeNodeLabel(king_lists_phylo_con, prefix = "*A")
```

```{r fig-phylo-rooted}
#| fig-cap: Rooted consensus phylogenetic tree
king_lists_phylo_con |>
  compute.brlen(method = "Grafen", power = 1) |>
  ggtree(layout = "roundrect") +
  geom_tiplab() +
  geom_nodelab(geom = "label") +
  hexpand(0.01)
```

## Ancestral state reconstruction

Using the rooted consensus tree, we can reconstruct the characteristics of the hypothetical archetypes at the base of each clade, including the basal clade – the putative original.
We use the maximum parsimony (MPR) algorithm.

```{r phylo-archetypes}
king_lists_archetypes <- anc_pars(king_lists_phylo_con, king_lists_phydata)
```

```{r tbl-phylo-archetypes}
#| tbl-cap: Ancestral state reconstruction for inferred archetypes (see @fig-phylo-rooted).
king_lists_archetypes$state |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("trait") |>
  mutate(
    trait = colnames(king_lists)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(!trait, names_to = "Ancestral node") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = trait, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(-`Ancestral node`, as.factor)) |>
  map2_dfc(rownames_to_column(king_lists), function(x, y) {
    if (is.factor(x)) levels(x) <- levels(y)
    x
  }) |>
  tt()
```

We can also use this to visualise the evolution of a specific trait on the tree – see below.

## Ancestral trait trees {.appendix}

```{r content, message=FALSE, results="asis"}
content <- map(
  1:ncol(king_lists),
  function(trait, king_lists_archetypes, king_lists, ...) {
    knitr::knit_child(
      here("maya_king_lists_asr.qmd"),
      envir = environment(),
      quiet = TRUE
    )},
  king_lists_archetypes = king_lists_archetypes,
  king_lists = king_lists
)

cat(unlist(content), sep = "\n\n---\n\n")
```
